title: The best touchscreen MacBook is already on your desk
content:
Macworld





Apple rarely arrives first to the party, but it tends to deliver an innovative twist when it eventually catches up to its rivals. AirPods, Face ID, Apple Watch, even the iPhone Duo weren’t the first of their kind, but they stood out for their leaps in design and functionality. However, as the launch of Apple’s first touchscreen MacBook Pro just proved, that’s not always the case.
Commercial touchscreen laptops have been around for almost two decades. Despite that, standard models have remained the default for valid reasons, most notably due to their perfect ergonomics. Instead of perfecting the formula as it usually does, Apple distracted fans with a recycled favorite—slapping on a glowing logo that had been retired a decade ago.
What makes the touchscreen MacBook especially baffling is how unnecessary it is. Apple already figured out the touchscreen setup back in 2019, and it’s been hiding in plain sight all these years.
Sidecar attachment
Sidecar was released as part of macOS Catalina in 2019. Billed as a way to expand your workspace, it essentially lets you use an iPad as an external wireless display for your Mac. Once it’s connected via AirPlay, you can drag Mac windows to your iPad’s screen and interact with them as you would on your Mac. Most controls were previously limited to Apple Pencil or mouse and keyboard input, but with macOS 27, you can use your fingers, too. There’s even a handy Sidebar on the ‌iPad‌ for common controls, like bringing up the on-screen keyboard or returning to the iPad’s Home screen, along with the Touch Bar that was previously included with certain MacBook models.

				
					

				
			
Sidecar turns your iPad into a wireless external display for your MacBook.

Apple




Unhinged design
Steve Jobs famously opposed touchscreen laptops because “after an extended period of time, your arm wants to fall off.” When reading early rumors about the touchscreen MacBook, I had expected—or at least hoped—Apple would do something different by incorporating an innovative hinge mechanism. A convertible form factor would have allowed users to interact with the touchscreen horizontally and easily switch back to the traditional laptop mode whenever needed. Alas, that did not come to fruition.
I acknowledge that we shouldn’t take everything Steve ever said as gospel because technology evolves, but many of his remarks still hold true today. The main issue with touchscreen laptops has never been weight or thickness, as some Apple execs recently suggested. At no point while using my MacBook does it feel natural for me to extend my arm and touch its display, and most people would probably relate. The new MacBook Pro is no different, and a sturdier hinge and lighter chassis don’t resolve the actual problem.
Sidecar is a whole different story, however. My iPad is untethered from the MacBook’s keyboard, letting me flexibly touch its screen horizontally or otherwise. This allows me to utilize touch input on macOS when the need arises without straining my arm. It’s precisely the kind of innovation Apple is generally praised for, and we’ve already had it for years.
Out of touch
The MacBook Pro with a PROLED XDR Display caters to professional creatives by letting them interact with macOS apps using their fingers. Yet, curiously, the machine is seemingly incompatible with many of these professional creatives’ go-to accessory: the Apple Pencil. This bars power users from taking advantage of precise interactions, pressure sensitivity, tilt detection, and all the other perks they cannot achieve with their fingers.
Meanwhile, Sidecar on the iPad supports Apple Pencil input—not to mention that iPadOS can run many desktop-class creative suites natively. So, whether you’re Sidecar-ing or using the iPad independently, you get to unlock advanced creation controls and workflows that surpass what you can do with the new MacBook Pro.
Beyond functionality, using an Apple Pencil minimizes fingerprints on your display, and creators know all too well how relevant that is. I’m far from being a professional photographer, but I’m constantly wiping down my 13-inch iPad Pro M4 before editing pictures because color correction and healing blemishes on the pixel level require that kind of clarity. Without Apple Pencil support, the new MacBook Pro’s display is going to get all smudgy as you attempt to get work done.

				
					

				
			
You don’t need a touchscreen MacBook if you already have an iPad.

Apple




Mac Duo
Another advantage for using Sidecar as a separate wireless monitor for your Mac is having two sets of app windows open on each screen simultaneously to work on more complex tasks. Touch Bar enthusiasts will also be delighted to learn that the discontinued MacBook feature lives on through Sidecar.
Non-MacBook Pro users, like those with a Mac mini/Studio, MacBook Air, or iMac, will especially appreciate being able to utilize the touchscreen without spending almost $3,000 on a new laptop—all thanks to Sidecar. In fact, it might be wiser to buy a Mac mini and an iPad Pro than a touchscreen MacBook Pro. Let’s break it down.
An M5 Pro Mac mini ($1,699) combined with an iPad Pro M5 ($1,199) costs $2,898—a dollar less than the touchscreen MacBook Pro (M5 Pro)’s starting price. With this package, you’d be getting one of the most advanced tandem OLED panels on the market and two desktop-grade processors instead of one, not to mention Apple Pencil support and far greater versatility.

				
					

				
			
Sidecar gives you the versatility you won’t get in a touchscreen MacBook.

Foundry




Pick a side
I’ve long depended on Sidecar with my MacBook Air, and—unlike the touchscreen MacBook Pro—it remains a prominent example of Apple’s classic “It just works” philosophy. The built-in feature requires absolutely no setup, cables, or technical literacy. Your Mac magically pairs to your nearby iPad and lets you mirror or extend the display wirelessly. That’s the epitome of touchscreen support on a laptop, even surpassing the highly advanced convertibles in terms of practicality and overall user experience.
Ultimately, if touchscreen laptops were truly essential, they would’ve evolved meaningfully throughout the past years, and Apple wouldn’t have waited this long to release one. Professionals have been using standard laptops for decades just fine, and add-ons like Wacom graphics tablets continue to thrive among digital artists due to their precision and horizontal designs.
Steve Jobs once said that people don’t know what they want until you show it to them. Apple already showed us the right way to do touch on a Mac with Sidecar, and it shouldn’t have caved to market pressure to build the wrong one.

title: Apple Releasing HomePod Mini 2 Tomorrow With These New Features
content:
Following more than two weeks of pre-orders, the HomePod mini 2 will begin arriving to customers and launch in stores this Friday, October 30.


Siri AI will be one of the HomePod mini 2's key upgrades, but the feature will not be available at launch. Apple said Siri AI support on the speaker will arrive in a future software update, but it did not say when the update will be released.

Siri AI is the more intelligent and personalized version of Siri powered by Apple Intelligence that launched on the iPhone 15 Pro and newer in September.

HomePod mini 2 is powered by the Apple Watch Series 10's S10 chip, up from the Apple Watch Series 5's S5 chip in the original HomePod mini. Apple said the S10 chip enables "advanced computational audio," but it did not explicitly confirm if the HomePod mini 2 has improved sound quality compared to the original model.

The speaker now supports faster Wi-Fi 6E, up from Wi-Fi 4.

new fourth-generation Apple TV 4K can connect to four HomePod mini 2 or full-sized HomePod 2 speakers in front and rear pairs, allowing for surround sound. Many home theater enthusiasts will prefer to use a proper 5.1 surround sound system with a center speaker and a subwoofer, but this basic all-Apple system at least exists now, and Apple says the front two HomePods virtualize the center channel to some extent.


You can mix and match HomePod mini 2 and full-sized HomePod 2 speakers for surround sound, so long as the front and rear pairs match. For example, you could have two full-sized HomePod 2 speakers as the front pair and use two HomePod mini 2 speakers as the rear pair. A related Whole Room Audio feature is offered for parties.

on Macs with Wi-Fi 6E and later. The full-sized HomePod 2 also supports this capability now — make sure to install the latest HomePod software version 27.2 via Apple's Home app.

There are three Siri microphones in the HomePod mini 2, down from four in the previous model.

Sound Glow feature, the top of the HomePod mini 2 glows and pulses in sync with the music playing. You do not need the new model, though, as a software update extended this feature to the original HomePod mini and the full-sized HomePod 2.

title: Up to 350,000 Macs exposed by a forgotten Popcorn Time updater
content:
An abandoned Popcorn Time updater left up to 350,000 Macs vulnerable to remote takeover, giving potential attackers a way to execute malicious code with full system privileges.

Popcorn Time
Security researchers at Eye Research detailed the discovery in an October 22, 2026, research report about Operation IXIM. The vulnerability affected Time4Popcorn, an abandoned fork of the popular BitTorrent streaming application that continued circulating under the Popcorn Time name after the original project shut down in 2014.
Some users had stopped using Popcorn Time, but its updater kept running. Eye Research discovered attackers could hijack it to install malware and intervened between November 2025 and March 2026.

title: Next Apple event: Expected dates and what Apple could launch next
content:
Macworld





Apple’s “Pro and Tell” media experience, took place in Los Angeles on October 28, 2026. The company announced its first touchscreen MacBook Pro, officially called MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, featuring tandem OLED, Dynamic Island and a thinner, lighter design.
It completed a week of announcements that included the iPad mini with A20 Pro on October 26 and the standard 14-inch M6 MacBook Pro and M6 iMac on October 27. Preorders are open, with availability beginning November 6.
Apple has not announced a date for its next event. Attention now turns to possible spring 2027 launches, although new products could arrive through press releases or another media experience rather than a keynote.
Apple’s annual event calendar typically includes WWDC in June and the iPhone event in September, with additional launches sometimes taking place in spring and October. Dates are rarely confirmed far in advance, but past schedules and reliable reporting offer clues for anyone planning to buy a new Apple device. Here’s everything we know about Apple’s next event, including the date, start time, expected announcements and what could follow.


When is Apple’s next event?
Spring 2027 is the next likely window for an Apple event, although the company has not confirmed a date.
Over the past decade, Apple has held spring events and media experiences on several dates:
March 4, 2026
May 7, 2024
March 8, 2022
April 20, 2021
March 25, 2019
March 27, 2018
Apple can also announce products without holding an event. In 2025, it introduced the iPhone 16e in February, followed in March by the seventh-generation iPad Air, 11th-generation iPad, MacBook Air and Mac Studio.
That makes spring 2027 a plausible window for further launches, whether Apple holds an event, invites the media to a hands-on experience or announces products through press releases.


						

							


What will Apple announce at its next event?
The iPhone 18 and iPhone 18e are expected to arrive in spring 2027, making them likely candidates for Apple’s next announcements. The iPhone Air 2 could also appear, although rumors suggest Apple may combine it with the iPhone 18 rather than release a separate model.
Other possibilities include a 12th-generation iPad with support for Apple Intelligence, expected in 2027, and an updated full-size HomePod. 


						

							


Will Apple livestream the next event?
Apple doesn’t livestream its media experiences, but for events like WWDC and the iPhone launch in September, it livestreams a keynote presentation.

Calendars at the ready.

Foundry





 FAQ 


1.
How far in advance does Apple announce an event?
Apple usually announces its events around one to two weeks before they take place, although the timing varies. The October 13, 2026 Experience was announced just five days in advance. Apple also sometimes chooses to announce products via press release without holding an event. 





2.
How long do Apple Events usually last?
Apple keynotes usually last between one and two hours and feature the CEO alongside various other Apple executives.
WWDC and the September event tend to be longer keynotes; the spring and late-fall events can be slightly shorter. 
For example, the September 2024 keynote event was 1 hour 38 minutes.





3.
What time do Apple events normally start in U.S., U.K. and other global time zones?
Apple’s keynote events tend to start at 10 am PT or 1 pm ET. That translates to the following times in the countries where most of our readers live:
U.S.: 10 am PDT, 11 am MDT, 12 pm CDT, 1 pm EDT
Canada: as above, plus 2 pm ADT
U.K.: 6 pm
Europe: 7 pm CEST, 8 pm EEST
India: 10:30 pm IST
Australia: next day — 1 am AWST, 2:30 am ACST, 3 am AEST
New Zealand: next day — 5 am NZST
The timings are generally the same for all Apple Keynotes, but can be slightly different if Apple holds the event during the period of a couple of weeks when the clocks have changed in the U.S. but not elsewhere.
Sometimes Apple holds events at different times, for example, in October 2023 the event was held in late afternoon in San Francisco, which meant it was midnight in the U.K. The event on October 13, 2026 started at 9 am in New York, 2 pm in the U.K.
If Apple doesn’t hold an event and instead just issues a press release, that usually happens around 8 am PT, 11 am ET and 4 pm U.K. time.





4.
How often does Apple hold events?
There can be as many as four Apple events in a year:  
Spring Event
WWDC in June
iPhone Event in September
Late Fall Event in October
This event calendar is by no means set in stone, though, with the spring and October events being less regular. Some years, Apple doesn’t hold a spring event at all. In 2025 Apple only held two events, preferring instead to announce new products via press release.





5.
Will there be a live stream at the next Apple Event?
Apple usually livestreams the iPhone announcement in September and the WWDC keynote in June.





6.
Does Apple ever announce products without an event? 
Apple frequently announces products without a keynote event, often opting for press releases or multi-day announcement windows. In recent years, the company has increasingly reserved its large-scale media events for major flagship launches, such as the primary iPhone lineup in September, while using press releases for iterative updates or “chip bumps” that may not warrant a full hour-long presentation.





7.
How to watch an Apple event
Apple events are typically broadcast across several digital platforms, allowing viewers to tune in from almost any device. While the company previously restricted access to its own hardware or the Safari browser, these barriers have been removed in recent years.
You can access live Apple presentations through the following official channels:
YouTube: This is often considered the easiest way to watch. Apple streams its keynotes live on its official YouTube channel, which can be accessed via any web browser or the YouTube app on smartphones, tablets, and smart TVs.
Apple.com: The company hosts a dedicated “Events” page on its official website. 
Apple TV App: The stream is available within the Apple TV app on iPhone, iPad, Mac, and Apple TV hardware. Keynotes are usually listed in the app’s lineup a day or two before the event begins.
Apple Podcasts: Apple also showcases its events through the Podcasts app on Apple devices, where you can watch the video presentation.
We usually run a Live Blog which will provide minute-by-minute text updates and analysis as products are announced.
Following the end of the event, detailed breakdowns will also be available on the Macworld Podcast, which can be found on Spotify, Soundcloud, and Apple Podcasts. 








Will Apple hold a spring event in 2027? 

				
					

				
			John Ternus: Apple’s new CEO.
Michael Simon / Foundry




Apple’s spring events have become increasingly unpredictable. The company has not held a traditional spring event since May 2024, although it did invite members of the media, including Macworld, to a “Special Apple Experience” in 2026. 
Rather than a keynote presentation, the March 4, 2026 gathering was a hands-on showcase that followed three days of product announcements, including the MacBook Neo, iPhone 17e, and M5 MacBook Air.
Will Apple take a similar approach to spring product launches in 2027? It’s certainly possible. The format appeared to work well, allowing each product announcement to receive its own media coverage rather than competing for attention during a single event. 
Apple is expected to release three iPhone models in spring 2027 – or it could be two new iPhones, with the Air and iPhone 18 merging.
iPhone 18 
iPhone 18e
iPhone Air 2
Apple may also update the MacBook Air with an M6 processor and the MacBook Neo in spring 2027.


						

							


When is WWDC 2027?

				
					

				
			
Foundry




When is the WWDC keynote?
In 2026 the WWDC keynote was on Monday June 8. In 2025 it started on Monday June 9. We expect WWDC will start on Monday 7 June in 2027. 
WWDC generally runs from the Monday to Friday in the second week of June. 
What Apple could launch at WWDC
WWDC is Apple’s big developer event at which it reveals plans for the operating systems that run on Apple hardware.
In June 2027 we expect Apple to unveil details of iOS 28, iPadOS 28, macOS 28, updates to watchOS, tvOS, HomePod software, and an update to Apple’s visionOS.
Apple sometimes announces new hardware at WWDC, usually the high-end models targeted at power users, so we could see new Macs.
Following the keynote on Monday, developer events and sessions will run throughout the week. You can read more about WWDC date, times and everything you need to know in a separate article.


						

							




Apple event calendar 2026: What did Apple launch in 2026?
Apple held five events and hands-on media experiences in 2026, alongside several launches via press release:
March 4: Hands-on experiences followed announcements of the iPhone 17e, M4 iPad Air, M5 Pro/Max MacBook Pro, M5 MacBook Air and MacBook Neo.
June 8: WWDC introduced Apple’s upcoming operating systems, including iOS 27 and macOS 27 Golden Gate.
August: Apple announced new Mac mini and Mac Studio models via press release.
September 9: Apple unveiled the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, iPhone Duo, Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, and AirPods 5.
October 13: “Welcome Home” introduced HomeView, HomePod mini 2, a fourth-generation Apple TV 4K and the Apple Home Collection of smart-home accessories.
October 28: “Pro and Tell” showcased the touchscreen MacBook Pro, plus the M6 MacBook Pro, M6 iMac and iPad mini announced earlier that week.

In 2023 there were three events: WWDC in June, an iPhone event in September, and Apple’s second fall event on October 30 (or after midnight on October 31 if you weren’t in the U.S.).

title: New Apple products coming in 2027: What’s next?
content:
Macworld





It’s been a huge year for Apple, with new products arriving throughout 2026. March brought the MacBook Neo and iPhone 17e, followed by the new Mac mini and Mac Studio in August.
September delivered another wave of launches at Apple’s “Surprise and Shine” event, including the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, iPhone Duo, Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, and AirPods 5.
Apple turned its attention to the smart home at its “Welcome Home” gathering on October 13, unveiling HomeView, HomePod mini 2, a new Apple TV 4K and the Apple Home Collection. More announcements followed: a new iPad mini on October 26, then a 14-inch MacBook Pro and iMac with M6 chips on October 27.
Apple completed that week’s announcements on October 28 with the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display – its first touchscreen Mac. The new 14-inch and 16-inch models feature tandem OLED displays, Dynamic Island and thinner, lighter designs. Preorders are open, with availability beginning November 6.
What will Apple announce next?
With the touchscreen MacBook Pro now announced, attention turns to Apple’s 2027 lineup. Reports point to a spring launch for the standard iPhone 18, iPhone 18e and potentially an updated iPhone Air, alongside a new entry-level iPad with Apple Intelligence support. 
Apple’s roadmap: At a glance
As of September 1, 2026, Apple’s roadmap has come under the direction of CEO John Ternus. Former CEO Tim Cook has moved into the executive chairman role. The shift from an operations-focused leader to one with deep hardware engineering roots could signal a more product-driven approach – and a renewed emphasis on standout hardware.

Read on to find out what new products to expect at Apple’s next event and in 2027 and beyond.


						

							


Every New Apple Product Launching in 2027 and beyond
In the sections below we’ve split the upcoming new products into categories including Mac, iPad, iPhone, Apple Watch, Home, AirPods, and some new product categories.

The cameras are said to include both visible-light and infrared sensors, but they reportedly won’t be designed for taking photos or recording video, as their placement and image quality would make them unsuitable for those tasks. title: How macOS Adapts Its Controls for Touch on the New MacBook Pro
content:
Apple announced a new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display on Wednesday. It's Apple's first Mac with a screen that supports touch, and demonstrations Apple gave to the media show how macOS reshapes its controls for finger input. Menu bar items expand under a fingertip, window controls get bigger, and the Dynamic Island pulls down into a floating widget, amongst other changes.


Back in 2016, then-senior VP of marketing Phil Schiller (now Apple Fellow) argued that putting touch on a Mac display would mean "totally redesigning the menu bar for fingers" – something he said would clash with pointer devices. Apple's modern solution, however, is more subtle. The menu bar looks the same, but when you move a finger over a menu item, it expands to let you make a selection with more precision.

The same idea applies elsewhere in the macOS interface. For example, the traffic-light buttons that control window size and position also get bigger when you touch them, after which you make your selection with a tap. You can also swipe up from the bottom of the screen to reveal a hidden Dock.

A Pull-Down Dynamic Island


Elsewhere, the new MacBook Pro replaces the notch with a Dynamic Island where Spotlight, Live Activities, and Siri AI live. You can pull down on the Dynamic Island to open an expanded version that floats on the screen like a widget, giving you access to Siri responses and Spotlight search.

Apple says macOS automatically translates touch into clicks, so many existing apps will work with touch right away – no developer updates required. Possible interactions include swiping to scroll a webpage, pinching to zoom in on a photo, dragging and dropping slides between presentations, and double-tapping a window to fill the screen.

pull-to-refresh gestures in apps like Safari, Mail, and Calendar, while code in macOS 27.2 added touch-specific gesture recognition in Safari, Notes, Photos, and Quick Look.

Precision Work in Pro Apps


It appears that touch isn't just for casual swipes either. Pro application features have also been updated to work with fingers, such as color grading in DaVinci Resolve and tweaking soundtracks in Logic Pro.

title: Russia orders Apple to surrender users' messages on demand
content:

Moscow at night (Credit: Evgenit/Pixabay)
Multiple firms and apps are already on this same list, including WhatsApp and Telegram, so it's not clear why it has taken until now for Apple to be added. It's a continuation of the country's moves to control users' messages, though, as it follows Russia's blocking of FaceTime in 2025.

title: Best Mac monitors 2026: The Mac compatible displays we recommend
content:
Macworld





The monitor might be the second-most important part of your Mac’s setup after the Mac, of course–you can’t use any desktop computer without one and even the 16-inch screen on the MacBook Pro feels cramped if you are having a particularly productive morning. Spread your work out by plugging in multiple monitors to your Mac and extending your desktop over a wider space.
Because you’ll spend a lot of time looking at the display, you’ll want to invest wisely. Not only will you want a monitor that provides a pleasing experience, but the quality of the images on the screen can also affect your work.
However, picking a new monitor can be daunting. Not only are there many manufacturers to choose from, but there are also lots of sizes, resolutions, and features to consider—and when we say lots, we mean lots. We’re here to help guide you while you shop, and we have some tips on what to look for in a monitor plus advice on how many monitors each Mac can handle.
Best Mac monitors 2026
These are the best desktop Mac monitors we have tested. We round up the best portable displays for Mac separately if you want to take a larger display out on the road or easily store one out of sight when you’re not using it.
We’ve included Apple’s Pro Display XDR and the Apple Studio Display, not because they are necessarily the best choice, but for comparative purposes.

There are two screen options with this affordable 4K display: matte (MA270U) and glossy (MA270UP). If you want the most vivid radiant picture with deeper blacks and brighter whites, go for the Nano Gloss screen. If you want to banish glare and reflections more so than with the pricey Nano texture glass on the Apple Studio Display, got for Nano Matte.
Some displays sell the stand separately so there’s an additional cost consideration, but that’s not the case here as the stand is included. It offers a great range of adjustment: -5 to 20 degrees of tilt, swivels 15 degrees left or right, and 115 mm of height. The display can also pivot 90 degrees to Portrait mode, a far greater range of motion than the Studio Display. 
The MA270U/P can connect to a Mac through HDMI or USB-C. The USB-C connection offers 90 watts of power so it can charge your MacBook at the same time. If you want to use the display as a connection hub, you need to connect to the Mac via USB-C. Its built-in spare USB-C port offers 15W of power output and the USB-A 7.5W. There are two HDMI ports so you can connect to another device for multitasking.
The one thing that’s immediately noticeable with the MA270U/P is its impressive image quality. Colors are full of life and the detail is excellent. One standout aspect of the image quality is how sharp text appears. This is great for production and design work, but it can even make it more enjoyable to read and write.
It offers image quality that could satisfy users in a production environment–that’s one way of saying that its quality is better than what general users usually get. You might be able to find a 27-inch 4K display that’s a little cheaper, but it won’t look this good.–Roman Loyola

It’s just an old panel, with poor motion clarity from a slow pixel response and a complete lack of modern expected display properties. You’re not going to get a top-of-the-range display for that price, and the E27u does lack a few added extras, such as a built-in webcam or speakers. It gets all the basics right, though, with good image quality, multiple video inputs, and a useful built-in USB hub. The display’s 250 nits brightness may be relatively modest, but we found that the E27u looks bright and sharp enough for working with productivity software such as Microsoft Office, and also for streaming video from the BBC iPlayer and Apple TV+. And while Apple charges an extra £400 for an upgrade that allows you to adjust the height of its Studio Display—which is more than the entire cost of the E27u—you can tilt, swivel and adjust the height of the E27u, and even rotate it into upright (portrait) mode at no extra cost.
The E27u includes HDMI, DisplayPort and USB-C interfaces for connecting to your Mac, with the USB-C port also providing 65W power to charge a MacBook or other laptop if required. When using the USB-C connection you can also use four USB-A ports to connect devices such a keyboard, mouse or hard drive, and there’s also a second DisplayPort interface that will allow you to daisy-chain a second monitor if required. Our only complaint is that there’s no audio connector that would allow you to connect headphones or a set of external speakers to the display – although HP does sell a special ‘speaker bar’ that bolts onto the bottom of the screen if you want to add audio ($43.00/£40.00).–Cliff Joseph

							
		
How we test monitors
Macworld staff and other contributors with decades of combined experience have tested the displays in this round up. 
We thoroughly test each monitor, evaluating clarity of the image, maximum brightness, contrast ratio, and color accuracy and color gamut and other aspects of image quality. Motion clarity is also important, especially if the monitor will be used for gaming or other graphical applications.  
We also look at the build quality as well as usability and connectivity, and any special features or modes on offer, especially any that require software that may, or may not work as expected on a Mac. 
Why you should trust Macworld
Macworld prides itself on our experience and expertise when it comes to all things Mac. We conduct in-depth reviews of numerous monitors annually. Our comprehensive recommendations undergo rigorous testing and evaluation by our expert reviewers, who adhere to both performance benchmarks and stringent usability standards.
Should I buy an Apple display for my Mac?
Apple sells displays for its Macs, and you could go with its offerings, which are included above, but its displays are a quite bit more expensive than what third parties offer. 
Buying from a different company may mean you may not get a feature that Apple offers, but it may also be a feature that you don’t need, depending on how you use the monitor. 
There are plenty of companies that have great monitors that you can use with your Mac, without having to take out a second mortgage. Our sister publication PCWorld has tested several displays, and we list their top-rated ones that we have been able to confirm work with Macs, alongside the monitors we have reviewed below. Here are our recommendations in order, starting with Apple’s most expensive.
Are there compatibility issues for Mac monitors?
There are compatibility issues for plain M1, M2 and M3 Macs, which, unlike M1/M2/M3/M4 Pro/Max/Ultra MacBooks, can’t natively connect to more than one external display. Fortunately, there is a solution and we show you how to connect multiple monitors to M1, M2 and M3 Macs in a separate article.
How to choose a Mac monitor
Display technology is a bit of a movable feast, with a lot of confusing jargon and technical features to wade through, as well as a variety of different interfaces and cables that are used by Apple itself and the various monitor manufacturers. So it’s worth taking a closer look at some of the factors that you need to think about when buying a monitor for your Mac.
Screen size
Size isn’t everything, as the saying goes, but it’s a good place to start. Your decision will be influenced by how much desk space you have, and how comfortable you are while using the display. Some people think that a big screen is best, but then when they start to use it daily, they find that it’s too big. And the same goes for customers who think a small screen is best.
If you’re looking for a size to start with for your own personal research, we recommend 24 inches—just like with Apple’s iMac. That seems like a good size for most people, and it’s easy to go up or down from that point. Most people tend to go between 24 and 27 inches for home use.
For professionals—graphics, video, audio, even spreadsheets—a large screen will help you be more productive. Think 27 inches and higher. You’ll be able to fit more elements on the screen and not waste your time scrolling.
If on-screen real estate is valuable to you, consider a multi-display setup. A smaller screen can be used for things like chat, email, web, and more, while the bigger screen is your main workspace. Or get screens of the same size and maximize the space.
Screen resolution
Screen resolution can go hand-in-hand with screen size. Screen resolution refers to the number of pixels used to create what you see on the screen. The higher the resolution, the more detail you can see. Larger displays tend to have more resolution options, as well as the ability to support higher resolutions.
Often, when you find two displays that are the same size but have a wide price difference, it’s mostly because of the screen resolution. Monitors with high resolutions are more expensive. For example, Apple’s $1,599 Studio Display is 27 inches, and it has a high screen resolution of 5120×2880 (5K resolution). On the other hand, LG sells the 27-inch 27UK650-W, but it’s a 3840×2160 (4K) resolution display for content creators, and it’s $350–lower resolution, but $1,249 cheaper. (There actually aren’t other 27-inch 5K monitors available, except for the $1,449 LG UltraFine 27MD5KL-B.)
So what screen resolution should you get? Here are some suggestions; these are guidelines that you can adjust based on your preferences.
For general purpose use, such as web browsing, email, media viewing, small photo and video projects and viewing: 1920×1080 or 2560×1440 (HD)
For more-involved content creation, productivity, and media viewing: 3840×2160 (4K)
For pro-level content creation, productivity, and media viewing: 4K or higher
Want to use an 8K monitor? Read How to connect an 8K display to your Mac.
Connecting a monitor to a Mac
How a monitor connects to a Mac can be confusing. The traditional HDMI and DisplayPort connectors used by many monitors are being replaced–or complemented–by USB-C and Thunderbolt ports. And though USB-C and Thunderbolt cables may look the same, there are actually some important technical differences between them, so it’s important to check which ports your new monitor uses and make sure you buy the correct cables and adapters.
Most recent Mac models have Thunderbolt ports, so if you buy a monitor that has HDMI or DisplayPort interfaces only, then you’ll need an adapter to connect to the Mac. This can get a bit confusing, but Apple does provide a list of the ports included on most recent Mac models so that you can figure out what you need.
Apple also provides a guide to HDMI and DisplayPort technology, which covers Mac models going right back to 2008, so that should provide all the info you need for all the Macs you use at home or at work. Less expensive monitors still tend to use HDMI and DisplayPort, and while it’s not too costly to buy adapters that will allow you to connect your Mac, we reckon it’s worth future-proofing your new monitor by getting one that includes at least one USB-C or Thunderbolt port.
If a display uses Thunderbolt to connect to the Mac, it may have additional USB-C or Thunderbolt ports so the display can act as a hub. In this case, If you have a device you want to connect to your Mac, you can connect it to one of the ports on the monitor, which is already connected to the Mac and probably in an easier location for access.  
Look for a USB-C or Thunderbolt connection with power delivery (PD) that can charge your MacBook. A 65W PD will be enough for a MacBook Air or 14-inch MacBook Pro, but you’ll need at least 90W for a 15-inch or 16-inch Pro.
Read our article on how to connect a second screen to a Mac which explains everything you need to know about how to identify which ports you have, the adapters you will require, and how to set things up.
Ergonomics
If you’re going to spend a lot of time sitting at a desk looking at your lovely new display then you need to keep ergonomics in mind. The ability to tilt the angle of the monitor back and forth, swivel it around for easy viewing, and adjust the height of the monitor in order to avoid an aching back or neck.
Some monitors can pivot or rotate in either landscape or portrait mode.
As a rough guide, there is a point at about 2 to 3 inches from the top of the screen that should be at eye level. Obviously, eye level varies from one person to another, so it’s important that you can adjust the screen for your own personal comfort. You may also prefer a monitor that doesn’t suffer from glare, or you will be forever repositioning the monitor (or your head) to compensate for that.
Other considerations
There are other considerations you’ll want to make when shopping for a monitor. A lot of these come down to personal preference or what you need for the work you do. They include:
Color space (gamut): The number of colors a monitor can show. Professionals need specific color spaces.
Refresh rate: The frequency when a screen is refreshed. Higher rates produce smoother animations.
Webcam: Some displays have a built-in camera you can use for FaceTime and other video conferencing apps, or to record yourself.
Speakers: If you plan on frequently viewing or listening to media, a good set of speakers makes for a better experience.
How many monitors does my Mac allow?
The number of external displays you can hook up to your Mac, depends on its M-series processor. In short, any Pro or Max M1 to M5 processor supports at least two monitors, but base M1/M2/M3 and Neo MacBooks might be limited to just one. See below for the full list and also a link to our tutorial about how to get round the limitations.
• If your Mac has a base (non-Pro or non-Max) M1 or M2 chip, or is the MacBook Neo, it is limited to using just one external monitor unless you follow our DisplayLink workaround tutorial.
• If your Mac has a base (non-Pro or non-Max) M3 chip, it can only use two external monitors if its own lid is closed (so not showing its own screen) unless you follow our tips in the link above.
• If your Mac has a base M4/M5, M1/M2/M3/M4 Pro or Max chip, it is limited to using two external monitors – add up to five using the workarounds.
• If your Mac has an M5 Pro chip, it is limited to using three external monitors – add up to five using the workarounds.
• If your Mac has an M5 Max chip, it is limited to using four external monitors – add up to five using the workarounds.

title: Apple’s new MacBook Pro finally breaks the grid
content:
Macworld





This has been a year of major change with Apple’s MacBook lineup. 2026 started with simple and limited choices, and it’s ending with a robust lineup that broadens the MacBook’s appeal.
When the year started, Apple offered the MacBook Air, the laptop for the general consumer, and the MacBook Pro, the choice for professionals with higher demands. Those laptop were effective in reaching a large part of the market, but it was missing laptops at the two ends of the market: the sub-$1,000 market where budget-conscious shoppers are at, and the ultra-luxury market where money is no object.
In March, Apple released the MacBook Neo, a $599 laptop (now $699) that instantly became a hit in the budget market. And on Wednesday, Apple went in the completely opposite direction with the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR, a laptop that’s the rich pro’s pro. You’ll pay top dollar for it–starts at $2,899 for a 14-inch model, and a maxxed-out 16-inch model tops out at $14,549. Regardless of how you configure it, the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR has top-notch features at its base, and it’s not difficult to find people who are willing to pay for it.
When 2026 started, a top-of-the-line MacBook Pro cost $7,199. What does nearly twice as much get you now? An OLED touchscreen display, a better sound system, a new design that’s about a pound lighter, and, just so everyone knows you have one, a glowing Apple logo for the first time in 10 years. 
What about the grid?
At the 1998 Macworld Expo, Steve Jobs addressed the need for Apple to simplify its overly complicated Mac lineup. He presented what’s been dubbed the product grid, made up of two product lines (desktop and laptop) and two customer markets (consumer and professional). It’s been attributed as the core of Apple’s success and a testament to its simplicity. The company doesn’t get bogged down in too many SKUs and customers can easily find their desired product.






But over recent years, Apple’s Mac market share has been somewhat flat. Any noticeable jump in sales during a quarter was offset by a downturn soon after. It’s been reported that Apple wants its Mac market share to grow, and to do so it has determined that it needs to be more aggressive towards the attracting the fringes of the PC laptop market. 
So it broke the grid. Instead of two options appealing to most people Apple needed to offer products to persuade those sitting on the fence to get off it and buy a MacBook. Now, there’s an affordable gateway into the Mac and an ultra-luxury option, along with the usual in-between options. Choices, choices.
The grid served its purpose but is now insufficient for a company the size of Apple. It’s time to move off it. What’s different now is that the MacBook Neo, MacBook Air, MacBook Pro, and MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display are distinct products with obvious feature separation. It doesn’t have the quaint simplicity of Jobs’ quadrant, but by expanding the grid, Apple has set up the Mac for a different kind of success—one that fills every need and leaves no wallet unturned.

title: MacBook Air, Pro and Neo batteries compared: Which MacBook has better battery life
content:

Measuring MacBook battery life in straight hours of real-world usage (as Apple likes to do) is not always an accurate metric for comparison purposes as so many use and environmental factors play a part. We can, however, rely on straight technical specifications to tell us the stated battery capacities of each MacBook.
Where Apple is secretive about iPhone battery specifications (see our list of iPhone battery capacities based on teardowns), the company does list MacBook capacities in Watt hours (Wh). We have trawled through the Apple product Tech Specs pages from 2009 to 2026 to bring you as complete a list as we can gather using official Apple battery declarations.
The watt-hour is a unit of energy equivalent to one watt (1W) of power utilized for one hour of time. it is calculated by multiplying the number of Amps with the battery voltage. The higher the number of Wh the longer a battery will last using the same application. Batteries will lose efficiency over time so don’t expect a 2010-era MacBook battery to still possess the same power as it did when it was new or more than a 2026 model, even if it had an originally higher Wh rating.
Read How to test a MacBook battery: see if it needs replacing & replace it.

Does the MacBook Pro have a better battery than the MacBook Air?
As you can see from the above battery capacities, the MacBook Pro features higher capacity batteries than the MacBook Air, although not by a truly significant margin.
For example, the 13-inch M3 MacBook Air’s battery was rated at 52.6Wh, while the 13-inch M2 MacBook Pro had a 58.2Wh battery.
The larger the laptop, the higher wattage is the battery—as they generally require more power to run the larger, brighter screens. The Air features a Liquid Retina display with 500 nits brightness while the Pro has a superior 1,000-nit Liquid Retina XDR display. The latest pro PROLED XDR Display MacBooks can reach 2,000 nits.
The newer MacBooks with more efficient processors will also gain extra battery life by not stressing the batteries as hard to complete the same tasks.
Apple claims that the current 13-inch M5 MacBook Air (53.8Wh) boasts up to 18 hours Apple TV app movie playback. The 14-inch M6 MacBook Pro has a higher capacity 72.4Wh battery and can keep going for 24 hours on the movie playback. The 16-inch M5 Pro has the same 24-hour video playback claim despite its 100Wh battery but it has to run the larger screen.
Battery life depends on many factors, particularly which and how many applications you are running at one time.

title: How Accurate Were Rumors About Apple's OLED Touchscreen MacBook Pro?
content:
Rumors about Apple's work on a touchscreen OLED MacBook Pro started in 2023, when Bloomberg's Mark Gurman said there would be a MacBook Pro with an ‌OLED‌ display and a touchscreen, but ‌OLED‌ rumors date back even further. 


We heard a lot about the new Mac over the last few years, and we thought we'd take a look back to see what was right and what was wrong.
OLED


2016 - In 2016, ETNews said Apple was considering ‌OLED‌ displays for future MacBooks.

 	
2019 - The Elec said Apple was in talks with Samsung about ‌OLED‌ displays for a future 16-inch ‌MacBook Pro‌.

 	
2021 - The Elec said a future MacBook would use an ‌OLED‌ display with a two-stack tandem structure, which is what Apple announced today.

 	
2023 - ETNews claimed Apple was sourcing OLED panels in 14-inch and 16-inch sizes for the ‌MacBook Pro‌, which turned out to be accurate.

 	
2023 - Apple analyst Ming-Chi Kuo said Apple would release the first MacBook with an OLED display by the end of 2024 at the earliest, which was incorrect.


Touch


2023 - Bloomberg's ‌Mark Gurman‌ was the first to report on a touch display. In January 2023, he said Apple was working on an ‌OLED‌ ‌MacBook Pro‌ with a touchscreen.

 	
2025 - Kuo said in September 2025 that the ‌OLED‌ ‌MacBook Pro‌ would have touch sensors integrated into the display panel's top layer, which was correct.


No Notch/Dynamic Island


2024 - Omdia said in December 2024 that Apple would remove the notch from the ‌MacBook Pro‌ "in a few years," replacing it with a hole-punch camera. The hole-punch aspect wasn't quite correct.

 	
2025 - In August 2025, Omdia said an ‌OLED‌ MacBook coming in 2026 would have an iPhone-like Dynamic Island cutout instead of a notch.

 	
2025 - In October 2025, Gurman said the ‌OLED‌ ‌MacBook Pro‌ would have a "so-called hole-punch design" with a "display area around the sensor" similar to the ‌Dynamic Island‌.

 	
2026 - In February 2026, Gurman described the ‌Dynamic Island‌ as interactive and able to contextually expand based on the app or Mac feature in use.


Hinge


2025 - Gurman was the first to mention a reinforced hinge that would keep the display from moving when touched.


Design


2024 - In November 2024, Gurman said the ‌MacBook Pro‌ would have a thinner design, which was accurate.

 	
2026 - In October 2026, Gurman said he didn't expect the ‌MacBook Pro‌ would be "significantly thinner," tempering expectations.

 	
2026 - In October 2026, he said the ‌MacBook Pro‌ models would be "significantly lighter."


Chips


2025 - In October 2025, Gurman predicted the ‌OLED‌ ‌MacBook Pro‌ models would use M6-series chips, and in November, he specified M6 Pro and M6 Max chips.

 	
2026 - In June 2026, Gurman said there would be no M6 Pro or M6 Max chips, and the ‌OLED‌ ‌MacBook Pro‌ would instead use M5 Pro and M5 Max chips.

 	
2026 - In September 2026, Omdia said the ‌OLED‌ ‌MacBook Pro‌ would have an M5 Ultra chip option, which was wrong.


Pricing


2026 - In March 2026, Gurman said the ‌OLED‌ ‌MacBook Pro‌ models would be more expensive and would be above the mini-LED ‌MacBook Pro‌ models, which was correct.

 	
2026 - Just a day before the ‌MacBook Pro‌ models were announced, Gurman accurately predicted the $2,899 and $3,399 pricing.


Naming


March 2026 - Gurman suggested Apple was working on a "MacBook Ultra," but he did hedge and say Apple might not use the Ultra naming.

 	
April 2026 - Macworld claimed Apple would release a ‌MacBook Ultra‌ in late 2026 or early 2027.

October 2026 - MacRumors' Joe Rossignol speculated that Apple could call the new MacBook the "MacBook Studio," but that didn't happen.


Launch Timing


2021 - In March 2021, DigiTimes said Apple would release ‌MacBook Pro‌ models with an ‌OLED‌ display in 2022, which was not accurate.

 	
2021 - In November 2021, The Elec said an ‌OLED‌ ‌MacBook Pro‌ would launch in 2025, but also suggested the launch could be postponed.

 	
2023 - When Gurman first reported on the ‌OLED‌ ‌MacBook Pro‌, he said it would launch in 2025.

 	
2023 - In March 2023, display analyst Ross Young accurately predicted Apple would launch an OLED MacBook Pro in 2026, but he also incorrectly claimed an ‌OLED‌ MacBook Air would come first in 2024.

 	
2024 - In November 2024, Gurman updated launch timing to "probably" 2026.

 	
2025 - In August 2025, Dealsite.co.kr said Apple would launch a ‌MacBook Pro‌ with ‌OLED‌ in late 2026, which was accurate.

 	
2025 - In September 2025, The Elec also said the ‌OLED‌ ‌MacBook Pro‌ would launch in the fourth quarter of 2026.

 	
2025 - In October 2025, Gurman updated his launch timing prediction to late 2026 or early 2027.

2026 - In February 2026, Gurman said the ‌MacBook Pro‌ would launch in 2026, though in April he went back to 2026 to 2027 and said the touchscreen ‌MacBook Pro‌ launch timing could slip to the end of his predicted window because of the chip shortage. By September, he updated timing to "later this year," and he mentioned a November 6 launch on October 15.


Not Rumored

Some features in the new ‌MacBook Pro‌ were never rumored and came as a surprise.

 	
Illuminated Apple logo

 	
Up to 16TB storage

 	
Revamped speakers

 	
PROLED XDR naming


Wrap Up

Most of the rumors about Apple's ‌OLED‌ ‌MacBook Pro‌ were right, and Gurman scored a win being the first to suggest it would also have a touchscreen. Launch timing was harder to pin down, partly because Apple's plans shifted over the years, and more recently, because of the ongoing RAM shortages.

title: Should you buy a MacBook Pro now? M6, touchscreen and older models compared
content:
Macworld





Apple has launched an M6 MacBook Pro alongside a new touchscreen MacBook Pro with M5 Pro and M5 Max chips. If you’re buying your first MacBook Pro or replacing an older model, now is a good time to consider your options – although we recommend reading independent reviews before committing.
If you already own an M4 or M5 MacBook Pro that meets your needs, there’s little reason to upgrade unless the touchscreen model’s combination of OLED, touch and lower weight appeals to you.
Apple increased MacBook Pro prices by $300 to $500 in June 2026, so discounts and refurbished models remain worth considering. For the best value, compare the non-touch M5 Pro and M5 Max models and any remaining discounted M5 stock with the new models. If your purchase isn’t urgent, it may also be worth holding out for Black Friday deals at the end of November.
The MacBook Pro is best suited to creative professionals, software developers, engineers and other power users who need sustained performance, a premium display, plenty of ports and high memory configurations. If your workload consists mainly of web browsing, office work, studying or light creative tasks, the MacBook Air is likely to offer better value at a much lower price.
In this guide, we’ll help you decide which MacBook Pro is right for you, explain the best times of year to buy, highlight today’s best deals, and consider whether a refurbished model or MacBook Air would be a better choice.


Should you buy a MacBook Pro now? 
Now that Apple has announced its latest MacBook Pros, there’s no need to wait for the launch to see your options. The M6 and touchscreen models arrive on November 6. If you’re considering either, we recommend waiting for independent reviews. If you need a laptop immediately, an existing non-touch M5 Pro or M5 Max model could still be a sensible purchase. 
Buy a MacBook Pro now if:
You’re upgrading from an Intel Mac: Apple is ending support for Intel Macs, so if you haven’t yet switched to Apple Silicon, now is a good time to do so. As Intel Macs reach the end of support, they’ll stop receiving security updates, leaving them vulnerable to newly discovered security flaws.
You need a new laptop: If your current Mac is broken, unreliable or slowing you down, there’s little reason to wait.
You edit video or create content: Whether you’re editing 4K video, working in Photoshop or Lightroom, producing music or creating 3D graphics, the MacBook Pro delivers the sustained performance creative professionals need.
You’re a software developer, engineer or AI professional: Compiling code, running virtual machines, working with AI models or processing large datasets is much faster on the MacBook Pro, particularly the M5 Pro and M5 Max models.
You need sustained performance: Unlike the fanless MacBook Air, the MacBook Pro uses active cooling to maintain peak performance during long exports, renders and other demanding workloads.
You need professional features: The MacBook Pro offers a Liquid Retina XDR or PROLED XDR display with ProMotion, HDMI, an SDXC card slot, MagSafe charging and higher memory and storage options than the MacBook Air.
You find an excellent deal: A discounted MacBook Pro can be a good buy if it meets your needs. Compare its memory, storage, display and processor with the new models before deciding whether the saving is worthwhile.


						

							


When shouldn’t you buy a MacBook Pro?
The MacBook Pro is an excellent laptop, but it isn’t the right choice for everyone. If you don’t need its extra performance or professional features, you’ll save money – and probably be just as happy – with a MacBook Air. There are also a few situations where it’s worth waiting rather than buying today.
Don’t buy a MacBook Pro now if:
You want a processor upgrade over M5 Pro or M5 Max: The touchscreen models retain the same chip options as their non-touch equivalents. The M6 Pro or M6 Max aren’t expected until 2027. 
You’re looking for the best price: With new MacBook Pro M6 models now here, discounts on the discontinued MacBook Pro M5 could be more attractive. Black Friday may bring further savings.
You mainly use your laptop for everyday tasks: If your workload consists of web browsing, Microsoft Office, streaming, email, video calls or light photo editing, a MacBook Air offers excellent performance for much less money.
You’re a student with basic computing needs: If your coursework mainly involves writing essays, researching online or creating presentations, a MacBook Air is likely to be the better value.
Portability is your priority: The MacBook Air is thinner, lighter and completely silent thanks to its fanless design, although the touchscreen MacBook Pro is lighter than its non-touchscreen counterpart. 
You’re on a budget: The MacBook Air delivers outstanding performance for most users while costing significantly less than the MacBook Pro.
For most people, the MacBook Air is the better buy. The MacBook Pro only comes into its own if you regularly run demanding professional workloads that benefit from its active cooling, more powerful chips, superior display, additional ports and higher memory options.


						

							




Should I buy a MacBook Pro: At a glance


Your situationOur recommendation

Intel Mac or an older Mac that struggles with workConsider upgrading; choose the configuration around the workload
M1, M2 or M3 MacBook ProUpgrade if performance, memory, battery or display is limiting you
M4/M5 model working wellKeep it unless the new screen and design solve a specific need
Want OLED and touchCompare PROLED XDR models; read reviews before committing
Need Pro/Max performance without touchCompare the non-touch range
Want the lowest priceCompare clearance, refurbished and Black Friday offers
Mainly everyday computingConsider Air or Neo before paying for a Pro

 






MacBook Pro: Current line up
Apple’s MacBook Pro range now offers three main choices: the entry-level 14-inch M6, the non-touchscreen M5 Pro and M5 Max models, and the new M5 Pro and M5 Max models with PROLED XDR touchscreen displays. Retailers may also have remaining stock of the previous entry-level M5 MacBook Pro.
MacBook Pro M6
Introduced in October 2026, the 14-inch M6 is the entry-level MacBook Pro. It starts with a 12-core CPU, 12-core GPU, 16GB of unified memory and 1TB of storage. It retains the previous model’s design and non-touch Liquid Retina XDR display, while adding the M6 processor, Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. Choose it if you want the Pro’s display, ports and active cooling without paying for an M5 Pro or M5 Max configuration. From $1,999/£1,999. 
$1999 at  Apple						
					


						

							


MacBook Pro M5 Pro & M5 Max
Launched in March 2026, these models introduced Apple’s Fusion Architecture, combining two 3nm dies into a single system-on-chip. They offer:
M5 Pro: up to 18-core CPU (6 super cores, 12 performance cores).
M5 Max: up to 40-core GPU, up to 128GB RAM, and up to 8TB storage.
Thunderbolt 5, Wi-Fi 7, and Bluetooth 6 via Apple’s N1 wireless chip.
Battery life: 22 hours (14-inch M5 Pro), 24 hours (16-inch models).

MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display 
The touchscreen MacBook Pro costs $400/£400 more than an equivalent non-touch M5 Pro or M5 Max model. That premium buys a tandem OLED display, touchscreen input, Dynamic Island and a thinner, lighter enclosure.
It doesn’t buy a newer processor generation. Equivalent models retain the same M5 Pro or M5 Max chip options and Apple’s advertised battery-life ratings. Think of this primarily as a display and portability upgrade.
The extra cost may be worthwhile if you spend much of your working day using the built-in screen, particularly for visual work, or regularly carry your laptop between locations. If your MacBook spends most of its time connected to an external monitor, the non-touch version is likely to offer better value.

Is buying a refurbished MacBook Pro a good idea?

				
					

				
			
Foundry




Buying a refurbished MacBook Pro can be a great way to save money – particularly if you buy directly from Apple’s Certified Refurbished Store.
Apple Certified Refurbished Macs are typically around 15% cheaper than brand-new models and come with the same one-year warranty, 90 days of complimentary technical support, and the option to purchase AppleCare+. Every Mac undergoes extensive testing, is cleaned and inspected, and receives genuine Apple replacement parts where necessary.
The main downside is availability. Stock changes daily, so you may need to wait for the exact model, storage capacity, memory configuration, or colour you want. Newer MacBook Pro models also usually don’t appear in the refurbished store until several months after launch.
Third-party retailers, including Amazon, also sell refurbished Macs, but quality standards vary considerably. We generally recommend avoiding Macs that are more than five years old, as they may receive fewer years of macOS and security updates. In some cases, retailers also offer larger discounts on new, previous-generation MacBook Pro models during major sales events, so it’s always worth comparing prices before you buy.
For most buyers, Apple’s Certified Refurbished Store remains the safest and best-value way to buy a refurbished MacBook Pro.

Which MacBook Pro to choose
Choose the M6 MacBook Pro if you want Pro features such as the better display, extra ports and active cooling, but don’t need the power of the M5 Pro or M5 Max.
Choose the M5 Pro MacBook Pro if you’re a professional who regularly edits 4K video, compiles large software projects, works with RAW photos, produces music or runs multiple demanding applications at once. For most creative professionals and developers, the M5 Pro offers the best balance of performance and price.
Choose the M5 Max MacBook Pro if your work pushes a laptop to its limits. The M5 Max is designed for users editing multiple streams of 8K video, creating complex 3D animations, running large AI or machine learning workloads, or handling visual effects and other GPU-intensive tasks. Unless you regularly perform these types of work, the M5 Pro is likely to offer better value. 
Choose an M5 Pro or M5 Max MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display if its OLED touchscreen and lighter design justify the extra $400/£400. Choose between Pro and Max according to your workload; you don’t need the Max chip to get the new display.


						

							


What about the MacBook Air?

				
					

				
			
The MacBook Air is a good alternative at a lower price.

Stephan Wiesend




If you’re considering a MacBook Pro, it’s also worth looking at the MacBook Air. Apple updated the Air in March 2026, and with a starting price of $1,299/£1,299 (the price increased by $200/£200 in June 2026), it’s significantly cheaper than the MacBook Pro.
The MacBook Air is a good choice if you:
Mainly browse the web, use Microsoft Office or stream media.
Are a student or home user with light computing needs.
Value portability and a silent, fanless design. 
Want the best value MacBook.
However, the lower price comes with a few compromises. Compared to the MacBook Pro, the Air offers lower sustained performance, a less advanced display, fewer ports, and lower memory and storage limits.
Choose the MacBook Pro if you need:
Sustained performance for video editing, coding, 3D rendering or AI workloads.
A Liquid Retina XDR display with ProMotion and HDR.
More connectivity, including HDMI, an SDXC card slot and additional Thunderbolt ports.
Higher-end M5 Pro or M5 Max chips, with up to 128GB of unified memory.
For most everyday users, the MacBook Air is the better value. But if your work regularly pushes your laptop to its limits, the MacBook Pro is well worth the extra investment.


						

							


Do you need to upgrade your current Mac?

				
					

				
			
Apple




Whether you need to upgrade depends on three things: how old your Mac is, whether Apple still supports it, and whether it can keep up with the apps and features you use every day.
If you have an Intel Mac, it’s time to upgrade
With macOS 27 Golden Gate, Apple has ended support for Intel Macs. While Apple is expected to continue providing security updates for the small number of Intel Macs that support macOS 26 Tahoe, that support is likely to last only another year or two.
The only Intel Macs that can run macOS Tahoe are:
16-inch MacBook Pro (2019)
13-inch MacBook Pro (2020, four Thunderbolt ports)
27-inch iMac (2020)
Mac Pro (2019)
If your Mac isn’t on this list, it may no longer receive the latest macOS updates and will eventually stop receiving security updates. For more advice, read How long Macs and MacBooks last: Lifespan, support and when to upgrade.
If you’re still using an Intel Mac, we recommend upgrading as soon as your budget allows. Moving from Intel to Apple Silicon is one of the biggest upgrades Apple has ever offered. You’ll benefit from dramatically faster performance, much longer battery life, quieter operation, Apple Intelligence support, and many more years of macOS compatibility. Read our guides to macOS Tahoe and macOS Golden Gate to see what you’ll gain by upgrading.

title: iPhone Duo: Turn the Hinge Into an App Launcher
content:
If you're eager to change your screen time habits – like staying off Instagram or reading more books – the iPhone Duo may offer a solution. It's the first iPhone with two screens, and there's a trick that you can use to make it consistently open a specific app whenever you unfold it and look at the bigger display.  


In the Shortcuts app, there's a new iPhone Duo trigger called "Opened or Closed" that runs an automated action when the device is unfolded or folded. One of the best uses for it, I've found, is launching a specific app the moment you open your Duo – so that unfolding the phone takes you straight into the app experience you're expecting, and nothing else distracts. 

I've always been keen to read more on my iPad, so in this example, I'll show you how to make the iPhone Duo launch the Kindle app whenever you unfold the device. It makes flipping the phone open feel like opening a book to where you left off. But you can substitute any app you like. The following steps show you how it's done.

  
Open the Shortcuts app on your iPhone Duo.

On the "All Shortcuts" screen, tap the plus (+) button in the bottom-right corner.

  
On the "What do you want your shortcut to do?" screen, tap Edit in the top-right corner.

  
Tap the Search field at the bottom of the editor, type "Automation," then under the "Display" section, tap Opened or Closed ("When my iPhone is opened").

  
Select Opened as the trigger in the editor screen, then search for the Open App action.

  
Tap the App placeholder in the "Open App" action, then choose the app you want to launch. In this example, we'll choose Kindle.

  
Now leave the Shortcuts app – the automation saves automatically and is active right away. You can rename the shortcut if you like, but it's not required.

That's all there is to it. Now when you open your iPhone Duo, your chosen app will launch automatically.

Closed as the trigger instead, or select Opened or Closed to run it both ways. The Shortcuts app also allows you to add conditions to an automation, like a time or a focus mode, ensuring that it only triggers when your chosen conditions are met.

title: Apple’s new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display: 5 top features
content:
Macworld





Apple on Wednesday announced the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, a new luxury addition to the high end of its MacBook lineup. Available in 14- and 16-inch models, the base price starts at $2,899/£2,899 and $3,399/£3,399, respectively. That’s $400 more than the comparable non-OLED models.
The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display reimagines the MacBook Pro with several features that appeal to the most demanding users. Here are the top features of the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display.


Touchscreen input
The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is Apple’s first touchscreen Mac. Now, users can tap on the screen in addition to typing on the keyboard and using the built-in trackpad. The touchscreen is in addition to these traditional input methods; it doesn’t replace them.
Users can use touch gestures that are familiar: scrolling can be done with swiping, pinch to zoom, double-tap a window to fill the screen, and more. Apple built the touch sensor directly into the display panel so latency is minimized.





				
					

				
			
Apple




The key to a successful touchscreen experience is accommodating software, and Apple has made several touch enhancements throughout macOS 27 Golden Gate. For example, Safari tabs “lift” and then enlarge as you drag it to a new location, then go back to their original size when dropped, and buttons enlarge when it sense your fingers on the screen.  Apple has also made system gesture APIs available so developers can configure their software for touch.



							


OLED display
The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is also the first MacBook to feature a tandem OLED display.  Two OLED panels are stacked together to provide an overall improved screen experience. Apple first introduced tandem OLEDs in the 2024 iPad Pro.
Marketed by Apple as a PROLED XDR display, tandem OLEDs produce deeper blacks, more contrast, and better colors. Apple rates the XDR brightness at 1,000 nits sustained full-screen, 2,000 nits peak for HDR content only, and an SDR brightness up to 1,000 nits sustained full-screen, 2,000 nits peak. That’s a big improvement over the mini-LED models.

				
					

				
			
Apple




Apple calls the display a “portable reference monitor,” a statement targeted at professionals who demand color accuracy. The laptop’s display engine controls color and luminance at the sub-millisecond level for content, pixel use, temperature, and environment. With support for ProMotion, the display supports variable refresh rates up to 120Hz. The new genlock feature syncs the display’s refresh rate with a connected camera’s capture rate.
Apple has also made structural improvements for touch input. A new hinge will provide better stability, and video stabilization is used to smooth the camera feed when using touch on a video call.



							


Dynamic Island
The new pill-shaped Dynamic Island is on the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, replacing the notch on the MacBook Pro. It acts just like it does on the iPhone, serving as a central area for Live Activities, notifications, controls, and other UI elements.

				
					

				
			
Apple




On the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, the Dynamic Island is the anchor point for Spotlight and Siri AI. When activating those features, the text window for user input opens under the pill box.



							


Thinner and lighter design
Apple has made the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display smaller than its MacBook Pro counterparts. At 3 pounds (1.4 kg), the 14-inch model is a half-pound (.2 kg)  lighter; the 16-inch model weighs 4 pounds (1.82 kg) and is .6 pounds (.31 kg) lighter.

The design also features the triumphant return of the glowing Apple logo on the lid. Introduced on the PowerBook G3 in 1999, the glowing Apple was replaced when Apple introduced the 12-inch MacBook in 2015. In 2016, Apple replaced it on the MacBook Pro.



							


M5 Pro and M5 Max chips
Like the MacBook Pro (which are not replaced by the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display and remains in Apple’s lineup), the new laptop comes with either an M5 Pro or M5 Max chip.
The M5 Max is Apple’s fastest chip in a laptop, beating the previous fastest laptop chip, the M4 Max, by about 12 percent in multi-core CPU and 7 percent in single-core CPU Geekbench 7 tests. Apple current fastest chip overall is the M5 Ultra, but its cooling requirements restrict it to the desktop Mac Studio.

Other new features
The  MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display also features:

title: Touchscreen MacBook Pro Guide: Release date, price and new features
content:
Macworld





Apple has announced its first touchscreen MacBook Pro lineup, officially called MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display. Available in 14.2-inch and 16.3-inch sizes with M5 Pro or M5 Max processors, the new models combine tandem OLED technology with direct touchscreen input. Touch is standard across the new range, while non-touchscreen MacBook Pros remain available.
The biggest changes include Dynamic Island, a smaller and lighter enclosure, and a new 16TB maximum SSD option on M5 Max configurations. The display adds Adobe RGB support and higher peak brightness while retaining a maximum 120Hz refresh rate. Other features include up to 128GB of RAM, Thunderbolt 5, Wi-Fi 7 and audio with a claimed 50% deeper bass.
The touchscreen models retain the same chip families, memory capacities and advertised battery endurance as their equivalent non-touch M5 models, making this primarily an upgrade to the display, design and how users interact with their Mac. U.S. starting prices carry a $400 premium over equivalent non-touch versions, with the 14-inch M5 Pro starting at $2,899 and the 16-inch M5 Max starting at $4,799.
What’s new compared with the non-touchscreen MacBook Pro?
The processor generation, maximum RAM, Thunderbolt generation, Wi-Fi/Bluetooth versions and Apple’s battery-life ratings haven’t changed, but there is a lot that is different. 


ChangeNew PROLED XDR modelsNon-touch M5 models

SpeakersRedesigned system; Apple claims 50% deeper bassSix-speaker system

 



Touchscreen MacBook Pro release date: When will it launch?
Pre-orders: October 28, 2026
On sale: November 6, 2026
Pre-orders opened on October 28, 2026, through Apple’s website and Apple Store app. 
Deliveries and retail availability begin Friday, November 6, through Apple Stores and Apple Authorised Resellers. Apple announces an initial rollout covering 30 countries and regions. 
Pre-order the touchscreen MacBook Pro PROLED XDR from Apple U.S.
Pre-order the touchscreen MacBook Pro PROLED XDR from Apple U.K.
Touchscreen MacBook Pro price
Apple has introduced a more expensive touchscreen range alongside the existing models. The new range carries a $400 starting-price premium over every equivalent non-touch M5 model. The premium does not buy a newer processor generation, more base memory or a larger entry SSD.
Apple 14-inch MacBook Pro PROLED XDR (M5 Pro, 2026)

Touchscreen MacBook Pro design

				
					

				
			
Apple




The new MacBook Pro retains a conventional laptop layout, built-in keyboard and Force Touch trackpad. It comes in Space Black or Silver, with an enclosure made from 100% recycled aluminium. 
Compared to the existing models, the weight reduction is more substantial than the thickness reduction: the 14-inch models lose 220g, while the 16-inch models lose approximately 310–320g. Slimmer borders also allow the larger screen to grow slightly despite a reduced enclosure footprint.
Apple describes a revised hinge and cooling system. It claims greater hinge stability during touch input and says the cooling design directs warm air away from the display. We’ll be verifying those claims in our review of the new laptop.

Touchscreen MacBook display

				
					

				
			The PROLED XDR Display isn’t just for touching.  

Apple




Both sizes offer M5 Pro and M5 Max configurations, and every PROLED XDR model includes touch. There is no base-M6 configuration in this touchscreen range.
OLED’s benefits concern image reproduction: individually lit pixels, deeper blacks and reduced blooming around bright objects. Touch adds a separate benefit – direct interaction with content. The maximum refresh rate remains 120Hz.
Apple indicates that pixel compensation mitigates ageing and burn-in, rather than establishing that OLED cannot deteriorate. It quotes 1% reflectance for standard glass; nano-texture scatters reflections further. 
There is also an oleophobic coating to reduce fingerprints. For cleaning, Apple advises powering down and using a soft cloth appropriately dampened for standard screens; never spray liquid directly onto the display. For nano-texture, use the supplied polishing cloth and follow Apple’s specific care instructions.
